_comment: Curated 'mechanics' library for the petrograd_1917 setting - see mechanics.py and engine.py's propose_mechanic_update tool. Each entry is a TYPE the AI may instantiate (never invent a type_key not listed here). seed_data is a historically-researched starting point the AI should use for the instance's initial `data` unless the campaign's own state already reflects divergence from history by the time it's created. Sourcing/precision notes are inline per entry - some figures are primary-source-anchored, some are reasoned interpolations between two anchored dates (marked explicitly); none are invented from nothing. canon_triggers (2026-09-09) names the canon_timeline.md beat(s) that make each type newly relevant or due for reconsideration - a structured hint alongside the freeform when_relevant text, not a replacement for it; see mechanics.catalog_prompt_section. 2026-10-26: render primitives are now validated in code (mechanics.validate_data), and three entries became 'hard' - the Soviet plenum and the Central Committee are seat_charts with per-bloc lean that operations.call_vote resolves by dice, and the garrison is a 'forces' order of battle that operations.sway_unit and resolve_confrontation read and write. The plenum and the garrison are seeded directly into new_campaign_state.json, so they exist from turn one; the others are still created by the GM when they become relevant (omitting data on create now uses seed_data).

petrograd_soviet_composition.label: Petrograd Soviet — Plenum
petrograd_soviet_composition.when_relevant: Exists from turn one (seeded in the starting state). Resolve any formal vote of the full Soviet with call_vote against it. Update it when the composition really shifts on-screen - a by-election wave in the factories, a regiment recalling its delegates, a faction splitting - and expect leans to move one step at a time. Expire only if the Soviet itself is superseded.

data_shape.body_size: integer - total voting delegates (must equal the sum of seats)
data_shape.factions: array of {name, seats, lean, note} - lean -3..+3 toward the player's side (+3 votes with the player almost always, 0 is persuadable, -3 almost never)
data_shape.influence_resource: fixed: the resource whose value nudges persuadable blocs (soviet_authority)

petrograd_soviet_composition.sourcing_note: Anchors: on 31 August 1917 the Petrograd Soviet passed a Bolshevik resolution on power for the first time, and on 9 September (Julian) a Bolshevik motion of no confidence in the Menshevik-SR presidium carried - commonly given as 519 to 414 with 67 abstentions - after which Chkheidze's presidium resigned; Trotsky was elected chairman on 25 September. The bloc sizes below are a reasoned reconstruction of a ~1,000-delegate plenum consistent with that 9 September tally (Bolshevik core plus sympathetic non-party soldiers and Left SRs on one side; defensist Mensheviks and mainstream SRs on the other; Menshevik-Internationalists in between), not a recorded roll call. Leans are design values: with no speech and average authority, the no-confidence motion passes most of the time but not always.

factions.name: Bolsheviks
factions.note: Swelling since Kornilov. Kamenev leads the fraction and wants to use the majority carefully; the district organizers want to use it now.

factions.name: Non-party soldiers' delegates
factions.note: Elected by regimental committees. Angry about the front and the officers, wary of any party - will follow whoever talks about peace and bread.

factions.name: Left Socialist-Revolutionaries
factions.note: Breaking from the SR leadership over land and the war. Natural allies, but they want to be partners, not followers.

factions.name: Menshevik-Internationalists
factions.note: Martov's people. Agree with much of the critique, fear a one-party seizure. Persuadable by argument, not by pressure.

factions.name: Socialist-Revolutionaries (leadership)
factions.note: Chernov's and Avksentiev's party machine, still tied to coalition with the government.

factions.name: Mensheviks (defensist)
factions.note: Chkheidze, Tsereteli and Dan's bloc - the old presidium. They built this Soviet and believe it must not become a Bolshevik instrument.

petrograd_garrison.label: Armed Forces in Petrograd
petrograd_garrison.when_relevant: Exists from turn one (seeded in the starting state). Every unit's loyalty runs -3 (fights for the Provisional Government) to +3 (fights for the Soviet); units at -1..+1 stay in barracks. Use sway_unit for the player's personal appeals and resolve_confrontation for any armed clash. Use propose_mechanic_update only for changes the fiction produces without an operation (a regiment's committee re-elected, reinforcements arriving) - the app limits loyalty moves to one step per update. Add units that arrive in the city (front-line troops, Cossack columns) with an update rather than inventing them mid-fight.

data_shape.units: array of {id, name, kind, strength, readiness 1-5, loyalty -3..+3, note}. kind is garrison | militia | naval | cossack | cadet | volunteer | armor - garrison units drive the derived garrison_loyalty resource.
data_shape.loyalty_scale: fixed description of what + and - mean

petrograd_garrison.sourcing_note: Unit list from the Petrograd Military District's garrison in 1917: the Guards reserve regiments (Pavlovsky, Keksgolmsky, Volynsky, Litovsky, Izmailovsky, Grenadier, Finlyandsky, Moskovsky, Egersky, Preobrazhensky, Semyonovsky), the Peter and Paul Fortress garrison, the 1st, 4th and 14th Don Cossack regiments, the officer-cadet (junker) schools, the 1st Petrograd Women's Battalion, the armored car units, the Red Guards (armed in large numbers during the Kornilov affair), and the Kronstadt sailors. Reserve battalions numbered thousands on paper; 'strength' here is an estimate of men who would actually turn out, far below the rolls. Loyalty values are a design reconstruction of early September 1917: broadly Soviet-leaning after Kornilov but not yet willing to fight for an insurrection, with the regiments that declared for the Military-Revolutionary Committee earliest in October (Pavlovsky, Keksgolmsky) a step ahead, the Preobrazhensky and Semyonovsky (who declared neutrality in October) and the Peter and Paul garrison (won over only on 23 October) a step behind, and the cadets and the Women's Battalion (who defended the Winter Palace) on the government's side. Treat all strengths as approximate.

seed_data.loyalty_scale: +3 marches for the Soviet unprompted · +2 fights for the Soviet when called · +1/0/-1 stays in barracks · -2 fights for the Provisional Government when ordered · -3 moves against the Soviet unprompted

units.name: Red Guards
units.note: Factory militias, rifles handed out during the Kornilov scare. Enthusiastic, badly trained, short of officers.

units.name: Kronstadt sailors
units.note: Baltic Fleet sailors from the island base - the most radical armed men in Russia. A day's movement from the city.

units.name: Pavlovsky Regiment
units.note: Its committee is solidly Bolshevik. Barracks on the Field of Mars, a few hundred meters from the Winter Palace.

units.name: Keksgolmsky Regiment
units.note: Radicalized, close to the Bolshevik Military Organization.

units.name: Volynsky Regiment
units.note: Mutinied first in February and is proud of it. Sympathetic, but won't move without a reason.

units.name: Litovsky Regiment
units.note: Joined the February rising early. Leans left; tired.

units.name: Izmailovsky Regiment
units.note: Soviet-leaning, committee divided between Bolsheviks and SRs.

units.name: Grenadier Regiment
units.note: On the Petrograd side, near the Bolshevik district committees.

units.name: Finlyandsky Regiment
units.note: On Vasilievsky Island. Sympathetic, not committed.

units.name: Moskovsky Regiment
units.note: Vyborg side, surrounded by the most militant factories in the city.

units.name: Egersky Regiment
units.note: Undecided. Its officers still have some hold over it.

units.name: Preobrazhensky Regiment
units.note: The oldest Guards regiment. Wants no part of a fight between socialists.

units.name: Semyonovsky Regiment
units.note: Crushed the Moscow rising in 1905 and hasn't forgotten it; neither have the workers. Neutral, watchful.

units.name: Peter and Paul Fortress garrison
units.note: Holds the fortress and its arsenal - tens of thousands of rifles - with guns facing the Winter Palace across the Neva. Wary of the Bolsheviks.

units.name: Don Cossack regiments (1st, 4th, 14th)
units.note: Experienced cavalry. Distrust the Soviet, but bitter at Kerensky for how he treated Kornilov. Their neutrality is for sale; their loyalty isn't.

units.name: Officer cadets (junkers)
units.note: Students of the military schools - young, disciplined, and the government's most reliable armed men in the city.

units.name: 1st Petrograd Women's Battalion
units.note: Volunteers raised to shame the army into fighting on. Loyal to the government, quartered outside the city at Levashovo.

units.name: Armored car units
units.note: A few dozen machine-gun cars. Whoever has them controls the streets for an afternoon - their committee hasn't chosen.

red_army_command.label: Workers' and Peasants' Red Army — Command Structure
red_army_command.when_relevant: Create this only once the canon 'Trotsky becomes People's Commissar for War; founds the Red Army' beat has actually fired (see canon_timeline.md) - this is a real successor structure to petrograd_garrison, not something that should exist alongside it from the start. A real gap between the old garrison mechanic expiring and this one being created is historically honest (the old structure didn't survive intact into the new one) - don't force immediate continuity if the fiction doesn't support it.
canon_triggers: Trotsky becomes People's Commissar for War; founds the Red Army
red_army_command.sourcing_note: Real historical structure: the Red Army was decreed 3 January 1918 (Sovnarkom) but only began forming from 23 February 1918; Trotsky became People's Commissar for Military Affairs in March 1918; the Supreme Military Council was established 3 March 1918 with three directorates (Operational, Organizational, Military Communications) - en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Military_Council_(Soviet_Russia). The later Revolutionary Military Council (Revvoensovet, September 1918) is deliberately not included here - it postdates this setting pack's currently-scaffolded canon timeline (which currently ends at the Red Army's spring 1918 founding); extend this entry if the campaign is later continued into the Civil War proper.

root.name: Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom)
root.note: The new Soviet government, which decreed the Red Army's founding.

children.name: People's Commissariat for Military Affairs
children.note: Trotsky's own commissariat, held alongside (in place of) Foreign Affairs from March 1918.

children.name: Supreme Military Council
children.note: Established 3 March 1918, days after Brest-Litovsk, to organize the new army's formation and defense. Chaired by Trotsky himself.

children.name: Organizational Directorate
children.note: Recruitment, unit formation, and the difficult work of building a real army from volunteer detachments and conscripts.

children.name: Military Communications Directorate
children.note: Logistics, rail movement, and coordination across fronts.

diplomatic_position.label: Peace Negotiations — Diplomatic Ledger
diplomatic_position.when_relevant: Create this once Brest-Litovsk negotiations become a live concern for the player (canon 'Brest-Litovsk negotiations begin' beat). This tracks the negotiating position as a running ledger, not a chart - a new development is a new entry appended via 'update', not a wholesale rewrite of the earlier ones, so the ledger reads as a real history of how the talks moved. Update it as talks progress, recess, or collapse. Once a treaty is actually signed, update it one final time with the real terms and their consequences rather than creating a new instance. Expire only if the treaty is later formally abrogated/superseded (historically, the Armistice of November 1918 voided it) - not simply because active negotiating stopped, since signed terms remain a standing fact the player has to live with.

data_shape.entries: array of {heading, tag, body} appended in chronological order - tag is a short date/status label (e.g. a date or 'Trotsky's strategy'), body is the actual ledger content. Prefer adding a new entry over rewriting old ones.

diplomatic_position.sourcing_note: Real timeline: Soviet Russia requested an immediate peace 8 November 1917; formal talks opened 22 December 1917 at Brest-Litovsk; Trotsky personally took over the Soviet delegation 9 January 1918 and pursued a deliberate 'neither war nor peace' strategy (refuse to sign, but unilaterally declare the war over) against Lenin's own preference to just accept German terms - a real, documented internal party fight, not invented drama. The strategy collapsed when Germany resumed its offensive 18 February 1918; the treaty was signed 3 March 1918 (the same day the Supreme Military Council was established - see red_army_command) on harsh terms: Russia ceded Ukraine, Poland, the Baltic provinces, Finland, and more - about a third of its population and pre-war European territory, and a majority of its coal/iron reserves and industry (britannica.com/event/treaties-of-Brest-Litovsk; history.com/articles/treaties-of-brest-litovsk). Only the negotiation-opening seed is below; the treaty's real final terms belong in a later 'update' once that canon beat fires, not in this initial seed.

entries.heading: Peace negotiations open at Brest-Litovsk
entries.body: Formal talks with the Central Powers began at the fortress of Brest-Litovsk, following the Soviet government's 8 November appeal for an immediate peace. German General Max Hoffmann leads the Central Powers' military delegation.

entries.heading: Trotsky takes over the Soviet delegation
entries.body: Trotsky, as Commissar for Foreign Affairs, personally leads the negotiations from this point - and deliberately slows them for propaganda value rather than settling quickly.

entries.heading: German territorial demands
entries.body: Germany is demanding independence (under German influence) for Poland, the Baltic provinces, and Ukraine - effectively stripping them from Russian control. General Hoffmann pressed these terms firmly once talks resumed after Trotsky's own requested recess.

entries.heading: 'Neither war nor peace'
entries.body: Trotsky's own position, over Lenin's objections: refuse to sign these terms, but also unilaterally declare the war over and demobilize - betting that a wider European revolution makes the treaty irrelevant before Germany can enforce it. A genuinely contested call within the party, not Lenin's preference.

bolshevik_central_committee.label: Bolshevik Central Committee — The Question of Insurrection
bolshevik_central_committee.when_relevant: Create this (omit data to use the seed) when the Central Committee actually meets on the question of armed insurrection - historically 10 October, after Lenin's return. Its lean runs toward 'immediate armed insurrection', not toward the player, so call_vote needs motion_alignment (+1 for a motion to rise, -1 for a motion to wait). The player votes as a member (includes_player). Update individual members' leans as they shift on-screen; expire once the question is settled.

data_shape.factions: array of {name, seats (1 per member), lean, note} - lean -3..+3 toward immediate insurrection

bolshevik_central_committee.sourcing_note: Real meeting, 10 October 1917 (per marxists.org and wsws.org): about a dozen of the Central Committee's 21 total members met in secret, Sverdlov in the chair (Lenin's first meeting back from hiding). The resolution for insurrection passed 10-to-2, with only Zinoviev and Kamenev voting against - a real, public rupture, not invented drama (see their own npcs.md entries, written to voice exactly this dissent credibly). Trotsky himself is recorded as abstaining, not voting for - he held the rising should wait for the Second Congress of Soviets for legitimacy, a real tactical disagreement with Lenin even though he ultimately supported insurrection in principle. Other real attendees per the same sources: Stalin, Dzerzhinsky, Kollontai, Sokolnikov, Lomov, Bubnov, Uritsky, and Iakovleva (who took the minutes). 2026-10-26: converted from org_tree to seat_chart so the vote is resolved in code. Leans are design values from the recorded positions: Lenin and Dzerzhinsky the hardest for rising now, Kamenev and Zinoviev against, Stalin and Uritsky behind the resolution with less conviction. Trotsky is the player and is not seated - he votes through includes_player.

factions.name: Lenin
factions.note: Back from Finland in disguise. Every day of delay is a crime to him.

factions.name: Kollontai
factions.note: For rising, and a real ally of the player's.

factions.name: Sverdlov
factions.note: In the chair. The party's organizer - for it, and already thinking about how.

factions.name: Stalin
factions.note: Will vote with the majority. Says little about timing.

factions.name: Uritsky
factions.note: For it in principle, worried about the garrison.

factions.name: Kamenev
factions.note: Against. Believes a rising now will be crushed and take the party with it.

factions.name: Zinoviev
factions.note: Against, with Kamenev - and ready to say so in print.

military_revolutionary_committee.label: The Military-Revolutionary Committee
military_revolutionary_committee.when_relevant: Create this once the MRC actually forms and starts operating - the body mrc_authority (see resource_schema.json) is built to track, which starts near zero specifically because this organ doesn't exist yet at campaign start. This is the real operational instrument of the insurrection itself, distinct from both the Central Committee (which decides whether to rise) and the Petrograd Soviet (whose institutional authority it draws on). Update it as it takes on real operational functions or its authority visibly extends over more of the garrison/city. Expire it once its wartime function is complete and it's formally dissolved or absorbed into ordinary Soviet government organs (historically, within a few months of October).
canon_triggers: The October Revolution / storming of key institutions
military_revolutionary_committee.sourcing_note: Real structure per prlib.ru and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrograd_Military_Revolutionary_Committee: formed by the Petrograd Soviet in October 1917, formally chaired by Pavel Lazimir - a Left SR, which mattered for the optics of the Soviet (not just the Bolshevik party) acting - while Trotsky, as the Soviet's own President, was the real driving force behind it. Its membership was drawn from Bolshevik party representatives, Soviet delegates, factory and soldiers' committees, the Bolshevik Military Organization (Voenka), and the Red Guards - a real coalition body, not a purely party instrument. By the end of October it had representatives operating in at least 44 cities and 113 military units well beyond Petrograd itself.

root.name: Military-Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet
root.note: Formally chaired by Pavel Lazimir (Left SR) - real driving authority runs through Trotsky as President of the Soviet, but the Left SR chairmanship matters for the committee's legitimacy as a Soviet body, not a purely Bolshevik one.

children.name: Soviet Delegates
children.note: Draws directly on the Petrograd Soviet's own institutional authority - see petrograd_soviet_composition.

children.name: Factory and Soldiers' Committees
children.note: The base-level organizing network across the garrison and the city's workplaces.

children.name: Bolshevik Military Organization (Voenka)
children.note: The party's own dedicated military-organizing apparatus within the garrison.

children.name: Red Guards
children.note: The armed worker militia - see petrograd_garrison for its place in the wider military picture.
